titel: Reporting investment income: Forms 1099, 8949 and Schedule D
kurz: Which forms your broker sends, how the figures get onto your return, when correcting them brings money back, and how long you can still claim a refund.

bloecke.md:
In the US, no tax on investment income is withheld at the source as long as you have given your broker a valid Form W-9. Instead, the broker reports everything twice, to you and to the IRS, on information returns of the **Form 1099** family. You then report the income yourself on your return. The IRS compares the two automatically. If something is missing or does not match, it sends a CP2000 notice proposing additional tax, often a year or two later.

The 1099 is a template, not a final settlement. The broker only knows the account it keeps. It does not know your tax bracket, your other accounts, the cost of shares transferred in from another broker without data, or the value of inherited shares on the date of death. The gaps almost always work against you. Investment income reaches the return by three routes, which have to be kept clearly apart.

zeilen: Income reported on Form 1099
Interest, dividends and sales in a US account
Mandatory. The IRS already has the figures and matches them against your return.
Income without a Form 1099
Foreign accounts, interest on a private loan, sales of assets you hold outside a brokerage account
Mandatory as well. A missing form does not mean missing tax.
Adjustments on Form 8949
Missing or wrong cost basis, wash sales across accounts, inherited or gifted shares, employee stock
Your documented figures replace or correct those of the broker. This is where most refunds lie.

bloecke.md:
The first two routes are mandatory. Interest and dividends of $10 or more trigger a Form 1099-INT or 1099-DIV, but smaller amounts are taxable as well. Income from a broker abroad, interest a friend pays you on a loan and gains on assets held outside a brokerage account have to be reported from your own records. For these, nobody files anything with the IRS in advance, which is exactly why they are checked in an audit.

## No election needed for the lower rates

US law has no flat rate on investment income that you would compare with your personal rate. Instead, the return sorts the income into two groups. Interest, non-qualified dividends and short-term gains are ordinary income and are taxed at the regular brackets of 10% to 37%. Qualified dividends and long-term gains, that is gains on assets held for more than one year, are stacked on top of ordinary income and taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%. For 2026, the 0% rate applies up to a taxable income of $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly; the 20% rate starts above $545,500 and $613,700. Above a modified adjusted gross income of $200,000 ($250,000 jointly), the net investment income tax (NIIT) of 3.8% is added. These two NIIT thresholds are not adjusted for inflation.

The Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet in the Form 1040 instructions does the calculation, and tax software does it in the background. Nothing has to be applied for. What counts is that dividends are classified correctly and that the holding periods are right. A dividend is only qualified if you held the stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date.

bloecke.md: Capital gains and dividends raise your **adjusted gross income (AGI)**, even when they are taxed at 0%. Several other programs look at AGI or a modified version of it: the premium tax credit for marketplace health insurance, the income-related surcharges on Medicare Part B and D premiums (IRMAA, based on the return from two years earlier), the share of Social Security benefits that is taxable and the federal student aid formula. A large gain in a single year can therefore cost money elsewhere, although the federal tax on it is low. The tax return does not check these consequences; it only computes income tax.

## Corrections the broker cannot make

Form 8949 is where you correct what the broker could not know. In practice, this is the route needed most often. Six cases cover almost everything:

1. The cost basis is missing. Brokers must report basis only for **covered securities**: stocks acquired from 2011, mutual fund and ETF shares from 2012, most bonds and options from 2014. For older or transferred holdings, the 1099-B shows the proceeds but no basis. If you do not supply it, the IRS matching treats the entire proceeds as gain.
2. A wash sale crosses accounts. The broker only adjusts wash sales within the same account and the same security. A loss sale in your taxable account followed within 30 days by a purchase of the same security in another account, in your spouse's account or in your IRA is still a wash sale. When the purchase is made in an IRA, the loss is lost for good (Rev. Rul. 2008-5).
3. Shares were inherited. Their basis is generally the value on the date of death (26 U.S.C. § 1014), which the broker often does not have.
4. Shares were received as a gift. The donor's basis carries over, with a special rule for losses if the value at the time of the gift was below it.
5. Employee stock was sold. For shares from stock options and employee stock purchase plans, the 1099-B usually shows a basis without the part already taxed as wages on Form W-2. Without an adjustment, the same amount is taxed twice.
6. Dividends were reinvested or capital was returned. Each reinvested dividend was already taxed and adds to the basis; nondividend distributions in box 3 of Form 1099-DIV reduce it. For old holdings without basis reporting, overlooking reinvested dividends is the most common way to pay tax twice.

In 2026, you sell mutual fund shares for $20,000 that you bought in 2005 and later transferred to a new broker. The 1099-B shows the proceeds, the basis box is blank and the shares are marked as noncovered. From old statements, you can document purchases of $11,000 and reinvested dividends of $3,000 on which you already paid tax. Your basis is therefore $14,000.

If you report no basis, the gain is $20,000. At a 15% long-term rate, that is $3,000 of tax. With the documented basis, the gain is $6,000 and the tax $900. Two figures on Form 8949 are worth $2,100. Without the reinvested dividends, the gain would have been $9,000 and the tax $1,350, so this item alone is worth $450.

bloecke.md:
## How the forms fit together

The forms build on one another. The broker's consolidated statement is the starting point, Form 8949 lists the sales, Schedule D adds them up, and Form 1040 receives the totals. Form 8949 has two parts, Part I for short-term transactions (held one year or less) and Part II for long-term ones. Within each part, a checkbox states whether the broker reported the basis to the IRS, did not report it, or issued no Form 1099-B at all. Sales with reported basis and no adjustments can go on Schedule D directly as totals, without being listed on Form 8949. Adjustments are entered in column (g) with a code in column (f), for example W for a wash sale or B for an incorrect basis.

bloecke.md: Brokers combine Forms 1099-B, 1099-DIV, 1099-INT and related forms in one consolidated statement, which must reach you by February 15. Corrected statements often follow in March, when funds reclassify their distributions. Its sections follow the forms, so most figures can be copied over or imported into tax software. Filing early with an uncorrected statement often leads to an amended return.

Supporting documents are not attached to the return; you keep them. The IRS generally has three years from filing to assess additional tax, six years if you left out more than 25% of your gross income, and no time limit for a fraudulent return or no return at all. Records of cost basis must be kept as long as you hold the investment and for three years after the return that reports its sale.

## Deadlines

The return for 2025 was due April 15, 2026, or October 15, 2026, with an extension. A claim for a refund, for example through an amended return on Form 1040-X, must generally be filed within three years from the date the original return was filed or two years from the date the tax was paid, whichever is later (26 U.S.C. § 6511). A return filed before the due date counts as filed on the due date. If you never filed a return for a year in which tax was withheld, the refund is only available if you file within three years of the original due date. The IRS pays interest on overpayments at the federal short-term rate plus three percentage points, adjusted quarterly.

bloecke.unter: As of October 2026, for returns filed on time. A deadline that falls on a weekend or legal holiday moves to the next business day.

ereignisse.text: For 2022, the three years ran out in April 2026. Missed basis corrections and unclaimed losses for that year can no longer be turned into a refund.
The oldest year that is still open. A Form 1040-X can still correct a missing basis, wash sales across accounts and double-taxed employee stock.
April 15, 2028 falls on a Saturday, so the deadline moves to the next business day.

With an extension, the return was due October 15, 2026. Refund claims remain possible until mid-April 2029. It is the first year in which brokers reported gross proceeds of digital asset sales on Form 1099-DA.

schritte.text: Download the consolidated 1099 from every broker and bank, including accounts without activity, and wait for corrected versions if the broker announces them.
Compare the basis on Form 1099-B with your own records, especially for noncovered shares, inherited and gifted shares and employee stock.
Look for loss sales followed or preceded within 30 days by purchases of the same security in any of your accounts, including IRAs and your spouse's accounts.
Enter sales on Form 8949 or as totals on Schedule D, dividends and interest on Schedule B and Form 1040. Foreign tax goes to Schedule 3 or Form 1116.
Keep basis records until three years after the sale has been reported. Answer a CP2000 notice by the date it states, usually within 30 days, and send the documents that support your figures.

bloecke.md: Form 8949 cannot recover foreign tax withheld above the treaty rate; that requires a claim in the source country. Investment advisory fees and other investment expenses are not deductible for individuals under current law. Losses on assets held in an IRA or 401(k) are not deductible at all. Net capital losses offset ordinary income only up to $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately). The rest is carried forward without time limit, but the carryover ends with the taxpayer's death and does not pass to the heirs.

mitnehmen: The broker reports to you and the IRS on Form 1099, and the IRS matches the return automatically; income without a 1099 is taxable as well.
Qualified dividends and long-term gains get the 0%, 15% or 20% rates automatically; nothing has to be applied for, but a higher AGI can cost money elsewhere.
The most common refund cases are missing basis on noncovered shares, wash sales across accounts and employee stock whose reported basis leaves out the amount already taxed as wages.
Form 8949 lists each sale with an adjustment code where needed, Schedule D adds them up, and sales with reported basis and no adjustments can go to Schedule D directly.
A refund claim on Form 1040-X is generally possible within three years of filing; as of October 2026, the oldest open year for returns filed on time is 2023.

begriffe.text: Information return on which a broker reports sales of securities to you and the IRS, with proceeds, dates and, for covered securities, cost basis and wash sale adjustments. It must be furnished by February 15.

The amount from which the gain or loss on a sale is computed, usually the purchase price plus fees, adjusted for reinvested dividends, return of capital and wash sales. For inherited assets, it is generally the value on the date of death.

Security for which the broker must report the cost basis to the IRS: stocks acquired from 2011, fund shares from 2012, most bonds and options from 2014. For noncovered securities, only the proceeds are reported.
Form on which individuals list sales and other dispositions of capital assets, divided into short-term and long-term transactions, with codes and amounts for adjustments. Its totals go to Schedule D.
Letter in which the IRS proposes changes because the return does not match information returns such as Form 1099. It is not a bill; you can agree or dispute it with documents by the date it states.
